summary: Describes data structures and API support for Mobile IPv6 as an extension to the Advanced Sockets API for IPv6. Just as that API exposes extension headers and ICMPv6, this gives programs the same level of access for Mobile IPv6 components. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Programmers need ways to use a feature that lets a device keep its address while moving. This gives them the commands in their programming tools.

questions: how to use mobility headers in sockets
subtitle: Programming interface for Mobile IPv6 network operations

tldr.problem: Applications need programmatic access to Mobile IPv6 features such as Mobility Headers, Home Address destination options and Type 2 Routing Headers, but no standard socket API existed for them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends the Advanced Sockets API for IPv6 with data structures, socket options and ancillary data mechanisms to give applications access to Mobile IPv6 protocol elements.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now send and receive Mobility Header messages, Home Address options and Type 2 Routing Headers using standard socket interfaces, enabling debugging tools, partial kernel-user implementations, and user-level monitoring of Mobile IPv6 packets.

today: RFC 4584 is an Informational specification providing the socket API for Mobile IPv6. Mobile IPv6 support is implemented in many operating systems including Linux and BSD variants, though the extent of user-level API support varies by platform.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (defined in RFC 3775) introduces new IPv6 extension headers and a Mobility Header protocol to allow devices to maintain network connectivity while moving between networks. Applications and implementations need to access these new protocol elements, but the Advanced Sockets API for IPv6 only covered basic IPv6 and ICMPv6.

This RFC extends the Advanced Sockets API to provide the same level of access to Mobile IPv6 components as the original API provides for extension headers. It specifies data structures for applications to retrieve and set Mobility Header information, Home Address destination options, and Type 2 Routing Headers using socket options and ancillary data objects.

The target applications are debugging and diagnostic tools, implementations where part of Mobile IPv6 runs at user-level and part in the kernel, and policy applications that need access to protocol information at the application layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile IPv6 is a way for devices to keep working while they move. This document tells programmers how to use Mobile IPv6 in their socket programs.

sections.title: Protocol Elements and Data Structures
sections.content:
The RFC defines C data structures for all Mobile IPv6 components in the header file <netinet/ip6mh.h>. The Mobility Header includes fields for protocol type, header length, message type, checksum and type-specific fields. Eight message types are defined: Binding Refresh Request (BRR), Home Address Test Init (HoTI), Care-of Address Test Init (CoTI), Home Address Test (HOT), Care-of Address Test (COT), Binding Update (BU), Binding Acknowledgement (BACK), and Binding Error (BERROR).

The Mobility Header protocol number is 135 (IPPROTO_MH). Four mobility options are defined: Binding Refresh Advice, Alternate Care-of Address, Nonce Indices, and Binding Authorization Data. The RFC also defines Home Address Destination Option (option type 0xc9) which carries the home address, and the Type 2 Routing Header which contains the mobile node's home address for routing at the care-of address.

New ICMPv6 message types are defined for Mobile IPv6: Dynamic HA Address Discovery Request and Reply, Mobile Prefix Solicitation and Advertisement. Router Advertisement changes include a Home Agent flag and new Neighbor Discovery options.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC defines 8 message types for Mobile IPv6: BRR, HoTI, CoTI, HOT, COT, BU, BACK, and BERROR. It also defines Home Address options and Type 2 Routing Headers.

sections.title: Socket API for Home Address and Routing Headers
sections.content:
Applications access Home Address destination options and Type 2 Routing Headers using socket options and ancillary data. To receive Home Address options or Type 2 Routing Headers, applications call setsockopt() with the socket flags IPV6_RECVDSTOPTS and IPV6_RECVRTHDR. The received data is returned as control information in ancillary data objects.

For sending Home Address options (not recommended for user-level applications), ancillary data can be used to specify the option content for datagrams. TCP applications can use sticky options for all transmitted packets, which can be cleared by setting zero option length.

The RFC specifies the order of extension headers: Hop-by-Hop Options, Destination Options, Routing Header, Destination Options with Home Address, Fragment Header, Authentication Header, Encapsulating Security Payload, and Destination Options. Helper functions inet6_rth_init(), inet6_rth_add(), inet6_rth_segments(), and inet6_rth_getaddr() assist with Type 2 Routing Header manipulation.

Note that on a pure IPv6 system, packets with Home Address options or Type 2 Routing Headers (with segments left non-zero) will be dropped if the system does not implement Mobile IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs use setsockopt() to turn on receiving Home Address and Routing Header information. When those headers arrive, they come with the data using ancillary data objects. Helper functions build and read Type 2 Routing Headers.

sections.title: Mobility Header Access via Raw Sockets
sections.content:
Mobility Header messages are accessed through IPv6 RAW sockets. The kernel passes a copy of mobility header packets to receiving applications, similar to ICMPv6 processing. Depending on implementation, the kernel may process the mobility header in addition to passing it to the application.

To receive Mobility Header messages, an application opens a socket with protocol IPPROTO_MH (135): socket(AF_INET6, SOCK_RAW, IPPROTO_MH). Applications should set the IPV6_CHECKSUM socket option to enable checksum computation and verification by the kernel.

This mechanism enables applications to implement Mobile IPv6 signal processing at the user level, such as the Return Routability protocol or future authentication protocols involving mobility headers. The RFC recommends that implementations verify Mobility Header checksums at the kernel level, and that applications set IPV6_CHECKSUM for portability.

The /etc/protocols file should include an entry for the Mobility Header protocol: ipv6-mh 135 # Mobility Protocol Header.
sections.plainLanguage: Programs can open a RAW socket for protocol 135 to send and receive Mobility Header messages. The kernel handles the checksum. This lets applications do Mobile IPv6 work without modifying the kernel.
